title: One God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
subtitle: Learning the grammar of Nicene confession
summary: The baptismal commission and the Nicene tradition teach Christians to confess one God while distinguishing Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Simple analogies require care.

scripture.text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.
scripture.context: Read Matthew 28:16–20. The risen Jesus meets the eleven in Galilee, speaks of his authority, and commissions their teaching and baptism.

objectives: Identify the three named in Matthew’s baptismal commission.
Explain the distinction between biblical wording and later doctrinal formulation.
Recognize the limits of familiar analogies.
essentialQuestions: Why does Nicene theology distinguish person and divine being?
What does a diagram help us remember, and what can it distort?
How does confession shape baptism and worship?

sections.title: The biblical starting point
paragraphs: Matthew ends with a commission grounded in Jesus’ authority and accompanied by his promised presence. Baptism is described in relation to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is a biblical foundation for Trinitarian teaching, but the passage is not a dictionary defining every term that later theologians use. Reading it responsibly means keeping its mission and teaching setting visible.

John 17 presents Jesus praying to the Father, speaking of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. The narrative distinguishes the one praying from the one addressed. This witness belongs in a broader biblical account rather than being forced into a single-verse demonstration that ignores the actual relationship portrayed.

sections.title: A historical confession with a careful vocabulary
paragraphs: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan tradition confesses one God and speaks of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Its received formulation is associated with the councils of 325 and 381. The OCA presentation and Catholic Catechism identify this conciliar setting. This textbook’s broadly Nicene profile follows that tradition for educational purposes; it does not claim that all religious groups accept it.

In this doctrinal vocabulary, “person” distinguishes Father, Son, and Spirit; “being” or “essence” concerns the one divine reality. These terms serve the confession rather than turning God into an object that can be completely described. A beginner should first learn what the formulation protects: the unity of God and the distinction of Father, Son, and Spirit. Technical historical questions can follow with further reading.

sections.title: Diagrams are reminders, not explanations of God
paragraphs: A triangle can help a learner remember three named persons, but it cannot explain divine life. Water changing among ice, liquid, and steam can suggest that one individual merely changes roles. Three separate human beings can suggest three gods. The point is not to replace one imperfect picture with a supposedly perfect picture; it is to keep the confession’s boundaries clear.

The visual in this lesson is a comparison aid: one God; Father, Son, and Spirit distinguished; one confession in baptism and worship. It is original teaching art, not a historically authoritative depiction. Ask learners to repeat the doctrinal statement in words so the visual does not carry more meaning than the text supports.

sections.title: Confession in the life of faith
paragraphs: The baptismal setting joins learning to discipleship. A Trinitarian lesson is incomplete if it leaves readers only with a diagram and no attention to worship, prayer, and obedient teaching. The commission includes observing what Jesus commanded. A group may therefore examine whether its teaching cultivates the life to which the passage calls it.

Differences about the procession of the Spirit and the later Western addition to the creed require historical precision. This preview does not silently choose one wording as though every church uses it. Before local adoption, a pastor should confirm the church’s received creed and preferred terminology. Honest identification of that decision makes shared learning possible.

sections.title: Practice the distinction in words
paragraphs: Invite learners to identify the difference between the biblical sentence and the doctrinal summary. Matthew supplies the baptismal naming of Father, Son, and Spirit within a commission. The Nicene formulation supplies a received way of confessing the divine unity and distinction. Both can be studied closely without pretending that their genres are identical. A helpful teaching session allows a learner to say which kind of statement is being made and why it matters.

If a question reaches beyond the lesson, record it rather than improvising an answer. Terms about eternal relations, procession, and the history of conciliar language deserve more than an analogy offered under pressure. Careful limits model reverence and give a pastor a clear starting point for further teaching.

languageNote.meaning: A theological name for the confession of the one God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
languageNote.caution: The English word is not a quotation from Matthew 28. It names a doctrinal synthesis, not an independently verified Greek etymology.

consensus: Within the declared Nicene profile, one God is confessed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is a defined confessional baseline, not a claim of agreement among all religious communities.
disputed: Eastern and Western traditions differ over the Filioque and its authority. Technical accounts of persons and relations also need specialist review; no diagram resolves these differences.
application: Read the baptismal commission as a call to teaching and life together.
Evaluate an analogy by what it risks implying, not only by how memorable it is.
reflection: Can I distinguish biblical wording from the doctrinal terms used to explain it?
How does confession shape the way I pray?
discussion: Why might a vivid analogy teach an unintended idea?
Which received wording of the creed does your church use?

quiz.question: Who is named in Matthew 28:19?
quiz.explanation: Matthew names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the baptismal commission.

quiz.question: What status does the lesson’s diagram have?
options: An original teaching reminder with limits
quiz.explanation: A diagram supports memory and must remain subordinate to textual and doctrinal explanation.
